claims.text: Optimizing phosphorus content to 5–10 at.% will improve glass-forming ability relative to an otherwise comparable alloy containing 2 at.% phosphorus.
Optimizing phosphorus content to 5–10 at.% will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to an otherwise comparable alloy containing 2 at.% phosphorus.
Phosphorus optimization will alter short-range order.
Phosphorus optimization will increase atomic packing efficiency.
Optimized phosphorus content will enhance the high-entropy effect.
An enhanced high-entropy effect will increase atomic packing efficiency.
The proposed changes in packing will reduce the tendency to crystallize.
Phosphorus contents of 5–10 at.% will produce a 20% increase in glass-forming ability relative to the 2 at.% phosphorus baseline.
Phosphorus contents of 5–10 at.% will increase the thermal-stability temperature by 50 K relative to the 2 at.% phosphorus baseline.
The exact optimum phosphorus content may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing conditions.
The proposed beneficial phosphorus-content range is bounded between 5 and 10 at.%.
Failure of the 5–10 at.% phosphorus alloys to achieve at least a 15% improvement in both glass-forming ability and thermal stability relative to the 2 at.% baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted thermal-stability improvement is specified as an absolute increase of 50 K, whereas the falsification rule requires a relative improvement of at least 15%. No baseline temperature or conversion is supplied, so the success and falsification criteria are not directly consistent.
The hypothesis predicts a 20% increase in glass-forming ability, but the experiment uses 15% as the pass/fail threshold without explaining why a smaller effect constitutes confirmation.
